title: U.S. Teen Unemployment
author: Seth Sandronsky
content:
![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/08/Screenshot-2026-08-06-at-2.52.34-PM-680x477.png)

Photo by [Amir
Hosseini](https://unsplash.com/@mmpixz?utm_source=unsplash&utm_medium=referral&utm_content=creditCopyText)

The unemployment rate of U.S. teens (ages 16-19) was 14.6 percent in June
2026, compared with a jobless rate of 4.2 percent for the national labor
force, according to the federal Bureau of Labor Statistics. The U.S. labor
force participation rate for teens was 35.4 percent, or about 5.2 million
workers, in June 2026.

The U.S. labor force participation rate for teens was 41.2 percent, or about
6.1 million workers, in June 2025. What accounts for this decrease in teen
employment?

Are employers introducing Artificial Intelligence such as ChatGPT into the
labor market and increasing the automation of the labor process? Given that
teens are new entrants into the paid labor force, e.g., the last hired and
first fired, if employers can save money automating entry-level work, they
will.

Like automation of the cashier occupation in the retail industry, employers
can and do compel customers to use their unpaid labor on self-serve devices
that replace human employees. Using the uncompensated labor of customers
versus paying employees, especially entry-level teens, to serve shoppers is a
cost-savings for employers.

On the other hand, remote work also impacts employers' hiring and firing
decisions. The pandemic ushered in the growth of remote work as an employment
option, one that allows employers to in part shift their costs, e.g., paying
for office space, onto employees who work from home.

The U.S. labor force of 169.4 million had a participation rate of 61.5 percent
in June 2026. The lower labor force participation rate for teens of 31.5
percent, roughly half, is due no doubt to this younger age group attending
high school, compulsory across the U.S. until age 18, though some states set
the requirement at ages 16 and 17.

Meanwhile, official employment figures exclude rather than include categories
of workers. Who are these uncounted workers?

To count as unemployed requires that one actively seek employment. Job
seekers, teens and older, who stop looking for employment after losing it fall
out of the officially unemployed category.

Incarcerated individuals held in jails and jails are also uncounted in the BLS
monthly employment situation report. The U.S. is the world leader in locking
up its population, with racial minorities overrepresented.

"In 2019, Black Americans represented 14 percent of the total U.S. population,
33 percent of the total prison population, and 46 percent of the prison
population who had already served at least 10 years," according to the
Sentencing Project. Minority overrepresentation in jails and prisons
correlates with unemployment data.

Black workers for example are jobless at roughly twice the rate of white
workers. The Black unemployment rate was 6.6 percent in June 2026 versus 3.6
percent for white workers.

In the meantime, expanding employment for U.S. teens is not on the radar
screen of the two-party duopoly. Call that a middle finger salute to teens.

Instead, the U.S. political duopoly is focused, laser-like, on sucking up
donor dollars from corporations and the wealthy. The Citizens United decision
strengthened that giant sucking sound.

Movement politics can weaken that sound.
